messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Holt is a 34-year-old Navy officer, married, who presented for an initial psychological evaluation following a referral from his unit's medical officer. He carries himself with the composed bearing one might expect from someone who has spent years operating in high-stakes environments, yet there is something effortful about that composure now — a quality of maintenance rather than ease. He is soft-spoken in session, choosing his words carefully, as though he is still not entirely certain that what happened to him is something worth discussing.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Marcus was on approved leave visiting extended family in a coastal community in the Gulf South when a rapidly intensifying hurricane made landfall with little warning. He and several family members, including his wife's younger brother, were sheltering in a single-story home when the storm surge overwhelmed the structure. The water rose faster than anyone had anticipated. In the chaos that followed — darkness, the roar of wind and water, the press of debris — Marcus found himself separated from the others, pinned briefly beneath a collapsed interior wall in chest-high water, unable to determine who was around him or whether anyone was calling out. The smell in the air was a sour, fetid mixture of floodwater and the contents of a nearby liquor cabinet that had shattered in the surge. His wife's brother did not survive. Marcus did, pulled free by a neighbor who had heard him. He has described the hours that followed — waiting in a crowded emergency shelter, pressed against strangers, unable to account for everyone — as worse in some ways than the water itself.

In the weeks after returning to duty, Marcus noticed that his memories of the event did not behave like other memories. They came as images rather than narrative — a flash of dark water, the angle of a ceiling beam, a particular quality of light through a broken window — and when they arrived, he felt his body respond as though it were still pinned: his chest would compress, his arms would brace. What unsettled him most was the sense that the memory felt cinematically extreme, almost impossible to locate in his own biography. He has said more than once, with a kind of bewildered flatness, that it doesn't feel like something that actually happened to him. And yet his body insists otherwise.

He had come to believe, quietly and with some conviction, that he deserved whatever suffering came to him. His reasoning, never fully articulated until recently, was shaped by his survival — by the fact that he, a trained officer, had not been able to do more. This belief has not taken the form of dramatic self-recrimination but of something quieter and more corrosive: a sense that comfort or relief would be somehow dishonest, and that he ought not seek either. He began telling himself this in the shelter, and he has not stopped.

The practical consequences have accumulated over months. Marcus stopped accepting invitations from friends in his unit — dinners, social gatherings — until the invitations stopped coming. His wife has noticed the withdrawal but has interpreted it as grief, which is not entirely wrong. He avoids the commissary during peak hours when it is crowded, routing his errands to early morning slots, and he has begun timing his movements around the base to minimize the press of bodies. He keeps clear of any situation that might replicate the sensory texture of that night: he will not sit in dim rooms, will not enter spaces where he cannot see the exits clearly, and the smell of alcohol — present at any number of officer social functions — has become something he physically removes himself from, sometimes without explanation. His supervisor has noted his absences from unit social events, and there has been an informal conversation about whether Marcus is "still himself."

He has come to feel, with a certainty that surprises him when he examines it, that he no longer belongs anywhere in particular — not fully among his colleagues, not fully at home, not anywhere he inhabited before the storm. He describes himself as standing slightly outside whatever room he is in. What finally brought him to seek help was his wife asking him, plainly and without anger, whether he thought things would ever feel normal again. He did not have an answer. He is most afraid that the answer is no.
